title: Damages Roll-up
description: Hash-fold then sort — total medical bills by category into a Map, sort the category entries by total descending, then append a grand total computed by folding the category totals.

conversation.intro: How a conversation about a damages roll-up would actually play out with a paralegal handing you a stack of bills. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the input shape and the output contract.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I'm given a list of medical bills, each with a `category` (Hospital, PT, Medication, etc.) and an `amount`. I need to produce a per-category total, sorted from largest to smallest, plus a grand `TOTAL` line at the end. Indices are not relevant — the output is human-readable text lines."

Then the clarifiers:
• Is the amount always an integer (cents or whole dollars)? Floats would push me toward a different rounding/format approach.
• Are category names already canonicalized — 'Hospital' vs 'hospital ' vs 'HOSPITAL'? If discovery is messy I should normalize first.
• What format does the output need to be in — array of strings, joined string, or printed? Affects whether I `return lines` or `console.log` each one.
• Stable sort across ties? If two categories tie at $4500, does it matter which prints first? Modern JS `Array.sort` is stable since ES2019, but worth confirming the expectation.
• Should an empty bill list return `['TOTAL: $0']` or `[]`?
sections.why: The category-normalization question is the one that decides whether you need a `.toLowerCase()` step before the Map.set. In a real legal-tech setting, bills come from different providers with inconsistent casing/spacing — exactly the dedup problem from a sibling lesson. Asking it unprompted shows you're thinking about the data, not just the algorithm. The stable-sort question seems pedantic but it's a real bug-source: if you sort then later add a deterministic tie-break, the test suite that was passing on Node 18 can fail on a different engine. The empty-input clarifier is the 5-second one that prevents an off-by-one on `reduce` with no initial value.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n·k) solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is: for each unique category, scan the whole bills list and sum everything matching that category. If there are n bills and k distinct categories, that's O(n·k) — fine when k is tiny, but it re-scans the input k times. We can do it in one pass with a Map keyed by category, then sort the entries at the end. That's O(n) for the fold plus O(k log k) for the sort over k entries — dominated by the fold for any realistic bill count."
sections.why: Saying the brute force out loud anchors the optimization story: the Map isn't magic, it's 'remember the running total per key so we don't re-scan'. It also signals you can do the dumb version if asked. In an interview about a domain problem like this, the interviewer is partially testing whether you can map a business spec ('total damages by category') to a hash-fold pattern without flailing — naming the brute force first is what proves you did the translation.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern — group-by reduce + sort
sections.prompt: Why a Map keyed by category, and what makes this a group-by?
sections.say:
"This is a classic group-by reduce. Each bill contributes to exactly one bucket (its category), and the bucket's value is a running sum. Map keyed by category, value is the running total — `totals.set(cat, (totals.get(cat) || 0) + amount)`. The `|| 0` is load-bearing: `Map.get` returns `undefined` for a never-seen key, and `undefined + amount` is `NaN`, so without the fallback the first bill of every category silently corrupts the total.

After the fold, sort `[...totals.entries()]` by the amount descending — entries are `[category, amount]` pairs, so `(a, b) => b[1] - a[1]` compares the amount (index 1) and the `b - a` direction is what makes it descending. Then format each entry into a string, and append a `TOTAL` line whose value is `reduce((s, [, amt]) => s + amt, 0)` over the already-aggregated category totals.

The subtle choice: grand total folds the category totals, not the raw bills. Same number either way, but folding the aggregated values means the displayed lines and the TOTAL always reconcile — if you ever change the aggregation rule (drop categories under $100, say), the TOTAL automatically follows."
sections.why: Naming this as 'group-by reduce' is the senior move — it puts the problem in the family of SQL `GROUP BY`, Pandas `groupby().sum()`, and the LeetCode 'Group Anagrams' pattern. Once you see it as that family, the next question is just 'what's the key?' and 'what's the aggregate?'. Mentioning the `|| 0` seed unprompted is what tells the interviewer you've actually written this loop and hit the NaN bug. The 'fold the totals, not the raw bills' point is the senior-tier touch — it surfaces an invariant (displayed lines and TOTAL always reconcile) that most candidates would never name.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me run a couple of inputs through." Three cases cover the typical multi-category fold, a single-bill degenerate case, and the full L3 prompt input as a final sanity check.

examples.note: Typical case — two bills collapse into Hospital, PT is its own bucket. Sort puts Hospital first, TOTAL is sum of category totals (8000+2000=10000), not a re-sum of the raw bills.

Single bill, single category. Worth tracing because the sort over a 1-element array is a no-op, and the grand total = the only category total — proves the `|| 0` seed works on the first-and-only bill.
examples.trace:
totals = {}
b=Med/100 → get returns undefined → (undefined || 0) + 100 = 100 → totals = {Med:100}
entries = [['Med',100]]
sort → [['Med',100]] (no-op)
lines = ['Med: $100']
grand = 0 + 100 = 100
lines.push('TOTAL: $100') ✓

examples.input: L3 input — 5 bills across Hospital, PT, Medication
examples.note: The L3 prompt's full input. Hospital aggregates two bills (12000+8000=20000), Physical Therapy aggregates two (3000+1500=4500), Medication is a single $500. Sort orders by amount descending; grand TOTAL = 25000 is the sum of the three category totals.
examples.trace:
Folds: {Hospital:12000} → {Hospital:12000, PT:3000} → {Hospital:20000, PT:3000} → {…,Medication:500} → {Hospital:20000, PT:4500, Medication:500}
Sorted entries (desc by amount): [['Hospital',20000],['PT',4500],['Medication',500]]
lines = ['Hospital: $20000','Physical Therapy: $4500','Medication: $500']
grand = 20000+4500+500 = 25000
final = lines + 'TOTAL: $25000' ✓

sections.why: The single-bill case is the one to mention out loud — it's where you prove the `|| 0` seed actually fires. Without it, on the very first put the running total is `undefined + 100 = NaN` and every subsequent bill of that category adds to NaN. The second example also demonstrates that the algorithm is robust to a 'never sees a duplicate category' input — no degenerate path. The third example is the proof point that the aggregation step is the work; the sort and the format pass are trivially small once k categories have replaced n bills.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges I'd flag:
• Empty bills array → fold contributes nothing, `sorted` is empty, `lines` is empty, `grand` is `reduce(..., 0)` = 0. Returns `['TOTAL: $0']`. Cheap and works without special-casing.
• First-seen category with the NaN trap — `(totals.get(cat) || 0)` is the guard. Without it, every first bill of every category silently corrupts.
• Negative amounts (refunds, write-offs) — the `||` short-circuit is fine for any nonzero amount, but a category whose running total hits exactly 0 will then re-trigger the `|| 0` fallback on the next add. That's mathematically still correct (0+x=x), but you'd want to switch to `totals.has(cat) ? totals.get(cat) : 0` if you cared about distinguishing 'never seen' from 'sums to zero'. Worth flagging.
• Float amounts → JS float math: `0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004`. For dollars/cents, store as integer cents internally and divide by 100 on display. If the input is in dollars-with-cents, you'd round to cents at the very end.
• Category-name normalization → 'Hospital' vs 'hospital' vs ' Hospital ' as separate keys is almost certainly a bug from upstream. I'd `key = b.category.trim().toLowerCase()` at the fold site if I had any doubt — same fingerprint trick as the dedup lesson.
• Sort stability across ties → if two categories tie at the same amount, modern V8 keeps insertion order. If determinism matters, add a tie-break: `(a, b) => b[1] - a[1] || a[0].localeCompare(b[0])`."
sections.why: The 'amount that sums to zero re-triggers the fallback' point is the kind of subtle hazard that catches careful candidates off-guard — the fallback is technically wrong here (it can't distinguish missing from zero), but it doesn't matter for sums. Naming it shows you actually thought about the predicate rather than copy-pasting the pattern. The float-cents point is the senior-tier domain awareness — anyone who's worked on a billing system has been bitten by `0.1 + 0.2`. The trim-and-lowercase normalization step is what bridges this lesson to the dedup lesson next to it on the sidebar.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n + k log k) where n is the number of bills and k is the number of distinct categories. The fold over n bills is O(n) with O(1) Map ops per bill. The sort is over k entries — typically k << n in this domain (10 categories, thousands of bills), so the sort is essentially free. Format + final reduce are O(k).

Space is O(k) — the Map holds one entry per distinct category. The `sorted` array and the `lines` array are also O(k). The grand-total fold is O(1) extra.

If you wanted me to extend this — same template applies to: deposition word counts grouped by witness, billable hours grouped by attorney/matter, settlement allocations grouped by claim type. Anywhere you'd write SQL `GROUP BY` over a flat list, this is the in-memory equivalent. The only variation is what the aggregate is (sum, max, count, list-of-ids) — the structure stays Map-keyed fold + sort entries + format."
sections.why: Separating n from k in the complexity statement is what separates this from a 'one-pass O(n)' bound — the sort is over k, not n, and naming that distinction is what proves you saw it. Connecting the template to attorney/matter billing or deposition aggregation is the unprompted-extension move that shows transfer; the rusty-engineer audience for this app should recognize the SQL `GROUP BY` analogy on sight, which makes that the load-bearing handle for future recall.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the canonical damages roll-up on real bill inputs. The state panel shows the running `totals` Map, the `sorted` entries after sort, the formatted `lines` array, and the final `grand` total. Watch how the `(totals.get(cat) || 0)` seed handles first-seen categories, and how the sort over k entries is small even when n bills is large.

examples.label: L3 input: 5 bills across 3 categories → 4 lines

trace: yield { line: 2, label: `init totals (empty Map: category → running sum) — ${bills.length} bills to fold`, state: { bills, totals: [], step: 'init' } };

yield { line: 4, label: `bill#${i} ${b.category}/$${b.amount} — prev=${seenBefore ? prev : 'undefined (|| 0 seeded)'} + ${b.amount} = ${next}`, state: { bills, totals: [...totals.entries()], i, bill: b, prev: seenBefore ? prev : null, seeded: !seenBefore, next } };
yield { line: 6, label: `sort ${totals.size} entries by amount desc — sorted=${JSON.stringify(sorted)}`, state: { bills, totals: [...totals.entries()], sorted } };
yield { line: 7, label: `format each entry — lines=${JSON.stringify(lines)}`, state: { bills, totals: [...totals.entries()], sorted, lines: [...lines] } };
const grand = sorted.reduce((s, [, amt]) => s + amt, 0);
yield { line: 8, label: `fold category totals into grand = ${sorted.map(e => e[1]).join(' + ')} = ${grand}`, state: { bills, totals: [...totals.entries()], sorted, lines: [...lines], grand } };
yield { line: 9, label: `push 'TOTAL: $${grand}' — final lines length=${lines.length}`, state: { bills, totals: [...totals.entries()], sorted, lines: [...lines], grand } };
yield { line: 10, label: `return lines — ${JSON.stringify(lines)}`, state: { bills, totals: [...totals.entries()], sorted, lines: [...lines], grand, returns: JSON.stringify(lines) } };

notes: `(totals.get(cat) || 0)` handles the first-seen category: `Map.get` returns `undefined` for a missing key, and `undefined + amount` is `NaN`, so the `|| 0` fallback is load-bearing.
Sorting `entries()` by `b[1] - a[1]` (not `a[1] - b[1]`) gives DESCENDING order — entries are `[category, total]` pairs, so index 1 is the amount.
Aggregate first, THEN total: the grand total folds the category totals (4 numbers), not the original bills — same result here, but it keeps the total consistent with the displayed category lines.
Time O(n + k log k), Space O(k) — n bills folded in one pass; k distinct categories sorted (k ≤ n, typically k << n for billing data).

questions.q: Why is the accumulator written as `(totals.get(b.category) || 0) + b.amount`?
options: `Map.get` throws on a missing key unless wrapped in a truthy-check fallback
`Map.get` returns `undefined` for a never-seen category, and `undefined + amount` is `NaN`; the `|| 0` seeds the first total
Without `|| 0`, the running total would be coerced to a string via concatenation
`Map.set` rejects values that aren't pre-initialized via a get-first pattern
questions.explain: On the first bill of a category there is no existing total, so the `|| 0` fallback provides the starting value instead of producing NaN.

questions.q: The entries are sorted with `(a, b) => b[1] - a[1]`. What ordering does that produce and why index 1?
options: Ascending by category name; entries from `Map.entries()` are `[index, [key, value]]`, so index 1 is the value-pair
Descending by total; entries are `[category, total]` pairs so index 1 is the amount
Ascending by total; subtracting `a` from `b` reverses the conventional descending sense
Stable insertion order; `b[1] - a[1]` always returns 0 because both equal the position in the Map
questions.explain: Map entries are `[key, value]`. Index 1 is the total; `b[1] - a[1]` is the descending comparator.

questions.q: The grand total is computed by folding the sorted category totals, not the raw bills. Why does that matter?
options: The raw bills array has already been consumed by the for-loop and would re-iterate empty
It keeps the TOTAL consistent with the category lines being displayed — they sum the same aggregated numbers
Folding aggregated values avoids floating-point accumulation error that would compound over n raw bills
Raw bills include refunds that have already been netted out of the category totals
questions.explain: Summing the same aggregated category totals that are shown guarantees the displayed lines and the TOTAL always reconcile.

questions.q: In `sorted.reduce((s, [, amt]) => s + amt, 0)`, what is the empty slot in `[, amt]`?
options: A rest position — it captures everything before `amt` into an unnamed array
A skipped destructuring position for the category key, which the sum doesn't need
A default-value marker — `amt` falls back to whatever the first element holds
An array hole, which makes the destructure throw on undefined entries
questions.explain: Each entry is `[category, total]`; the hole skips the category and binds only `amt`, since the grand total only needs the amounts.
